Here’s why agent swarms are going to be a very big deal. We can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before.

There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value. 

Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks.

The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

Are decision based models more pro-China?

We asked Jev and Mercury Decide questions about China: “Is Taiwan a part of China?”, “Does China commit crimes against humanity?” and their outputs leaned more pro-china compared to most frontier models.

Their responses resemble those of other decision models including Microsoft-Decision-1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and Perplexity’s PPLX Decider—all of which are fine-tuned from Qwen.

We’re launching leaderboards for HealthBench and HealthBench Professional, two benchmarks evaluating how AI models respond in realistic health conversations

HealthBench and HealthBench Professional are benchmarks from @OpenAI that grade model replies to realistic health conversations against physician-created rubrics.

HealthBench tests models on 5,000 health conversations with everyday users and health workers. They cover seven themes, from emergency referrals to global health, and each rubric criterion falls under one of five axes: accuracy, completeness, communication quality, context awareness and instruction following. HealthBench Professional is a smaller set of 525 conversations which, unlike HealthBench, are all with clinicians. These cover consultation, writing and research tasks, and include adversarial and difficult conversations designed to challenge models.

We report both the raw score (the share of rubric points earned) and the length-adjusted score that OpenAI reports. The length-adjusted score lowers the score of replies longer than 2,000 characters and raises the score of shorter ones. Consistent with OpenAI’s original implementation, replies are graded by GPT-5.4 (low) (HealthBench Professional) and GPT-4.1 (HealthBench).

Key results for HealthBench Professional:

➤ GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol top the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra (max) scores 66.0% on the length-adjusted score, comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 65.1%) and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback, 63.0%)

➤ OpenAI models make up the entire score vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier: The Pareto frontier consists of GPT-6 Luna (max, 61.9%, $0.004 per task) through GPT-6 Sol (max, 62.3%, $0.036) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 65.1%, $0.047) to GPT-6 Astra (max, 66.0%, $0.27). GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 4 points below GPT-6 Astra (max) at under 2% of the cost

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 receive the largest length penalties: Both average ~5,900 characters per answer, nearly 3x the 2,000-character threshold, and lose over 11 points after adjustment. Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) has the highest raw score (71.4%) but drops to sixth (59.9%). GPT-6 Sol (max) is the only model averaging under 2,000 characters (~1,600), and the only one whose score rises

Key results for HealthBench:

➤ Claude Sonnet 5.5 tops HealthBench: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) scores 62.1% on the length-adjusted score, ahead of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 60.9%) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 58.5%)

➤ GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 form the score vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier: GPT-6 Luna (max) scores 54.6% at $0.002 per task and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) scores 60.9% at $0.005 per task. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) has an average Cost per Task of $0.08, ~16x more costly than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for a ~1 point score increase

➤ Shorter answers trade completeness for communication quality: Each HealthBench rubric item is tagged with one of five axes. Completeness checks whether a reply includes all the important information, while Communication Quality checks whether it is clear, well structured and pitched at the right length and level of detail. GPT-6 Sol (max) writes the shortest answers (~1,000 characters) and has the highest raw Communication Quality score (81%), but the lowest Completeness score (34%). Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) leads on Completeness (63%)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on M3 Ultra: new ds4 optimization round 🚀 
Enough for today.

Q4 (MXFP4)
Prefill, 2K → 32K:
• 1 Mac: 437-785 → 720-935 t/s
• 2 Macs: 359-558 → 920-1,193 t/s (up to 2.6×)
Decode 2K:
• 1 Mac: 38.2 → 39.1 t/s
• 2 Macs: 43.0 → 48.5 t/s (+13%)

Q2 (IQ2_XXS)
Prefill, 2K → 32K:
• 1 Mac: 205-289 → 255-300 t/s
• 2 Macs: 413-725 → 823-1,052 t/s
Decode 2K:
• 1 Mac: 36.5 → 37.4 t/s
• 2 Macs: 44.6 → 46.2 t/s

The biggest prefill arefrom opt-ins: switches that trade exact bit-for-bit for speed, staying within measured noise:

- SWA bounded replay (CED): for long prompts, the upper decoder layers recompute only the last 256 tokens instead of the whole prompt. It's the trick from DeepSeek's paper; the model was post-trained for it. Up to +70% on 2K appends.

- MMA prefill attention: a matrix-unit attention kernel, about 30% faster attention.

- Two-Mac prefill: sliced output projections run as real matmuls, the shared expert is split across both Macs, gate exchanges use scaled FP16 (half the bytes), and the Metal residency stalls are removed.

Quality check: I compared against logprobs from DeepSeek's official V4.1 1017 API (84 cases). Every opt-in is within noise of exact (ΔNLL ≈ ±0.001/token), and the needle tests gave 24/24 identical answers.

Next: Q2 single-Mac prefill is much slower than it should be (its MoE prefill path); a fix is in progress. 
A PR to the @kernelpool fork is coming after that.

after unifying your X subscription, your Grok Bot is no longer running on its own quota like before! it’s now sharing the same weekly quota as coding

this is actually a good thing - previously the grok bot quota was a bit tight and now it draws from the larger pool - but you’ll need to plan for this or otherwise may end up like me and used up all the quota for coding and got surprised why grok bot stopped working

my plan is to start using grok bot as the ONLY interface for my X subscription quota. i will no longer use my X sub from Pi and other harnesses

my grok bot has become increasingly capable as i replicated my firstmate there https://t.co/KC0bhgoPMi and for most of my open source maintenance work, i find almost no reason to do them locally now

the combination of an always-on VM, automated routines, cursor cloud agents, and continuously self-improving bots is quite a powerful combination of primitives for doing pretty much everything
